version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 0/1] mm, swap: only prefer nonfull clusters on synchronous devices

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/1] mm, swap: only prefer nonfull clusters on synchronous devices
series_items.patch_summary: The patch partially reverts a previous change that preferred non-full clusters over free ones for all devices, except synchronous devices like zram. It introduces a new function `swap_prefer_free_cluster` to determine whether to prefer free clusters based on the device's flags. This is done to improve write performance by keeping swapout batches contiguous and allowing writes to be merged.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with zswap and suggested adding a best-effort check for zswappability. The patch author's approach to preferring non-full clusters on synchronous devices is generally accepted, but the reviewer wonders if it should also be applied to zswap.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Nov 5, 2026 at 8:51 AM Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr> wrote:
>
> Commit 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters") made
> allocations fill the nonfull clusters of their order before taking a
> free one, on every device without discard. Since commit 3cedb745d354
> ("mm: clarify the folio_free_swap() for do_swap_page()"), an exclusive
> write fault frees the swap slot, so a workload that rewrites swapped out
> memory leaves holes in full clusters, which then go back on the nonfull
> list. Reclaim allocates slots one folio at a time, so a batch of folios
> gets scattered over those holes, its writes can't be merged and it is
> written with many small requests.
>
> So partially revert commit 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over
> free clusters") and prefer free clusters again, except on synchronous
> devices like zram: they don't merge I/O, so the contiguity of the slots
> doesn't matter to them, and filling the holes first keeps the free
> clusters for large folios.
>
> Fixes: 9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters")
> Suggested-by: Kairui Song <kasong@tencent.com>
> Signed-off-by: Alexandre Ghiti <alex@ghiti.fr>

LGTM for the most part:

Reviewed-by: Nhat Pham <nphamcs@gmail.com>

Quick comment below:

> ---
>  mm/swapfile.c | 19 +++++++++++++------
>  1 file changed, 13 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)
>
> diff --git a/mm/swapfile.c b/mm/swapfile.c
> index 189f04d8838f..1c1b5d0b724a 100644
> --- a/mm/swapfile.c
> +++ b/mm/swapfile.c
> @@ -973,6 +973,17 @@ static bool __swap_cluster_alloc_entries(struct swap_info_struct *si,
>         return true;
>  }
>
> +/*
> + * Prefer a new cluster over a nonfull one if the device needs discard, to
> + * spread out the writes, or if it is not synchronous, to keep the slots
> + * of a swapout batch contiguous so that its writes can be merged.
> + */
> +static bool swap_prefer_free_cluster(struct swap_info_struct *si)
> +{
> +       return (si->flags & SWP_PAGE_DISCARD) ||
> +              !(si->flags & SWP_SYNCHRONOUS_IO);
> +}

Side note - I wonder if it's worth it to also prefer non-full clusters
for zswap as well?

It's a bit tricky, but I suppose you can do a best-effort check of the
folio's cgroup's zswappability?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch series addresses a performance regression in Linux kernel version 7.3, which increased swap I/O requests by up to 59% on certain devices. The issue arises from the interaction between two commits: one that prefers non-full clusters over free ones and another that frees swap slots on exclusive write faults. The patch series proposes to only prefer non-full clusters on synchronous devices like zram, where filling holes first keeps free clusters available for large folios.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to standardize the use of non-null attributes across the kernel by replacing raw compiler attributes with the __nonnull_args() macro. The first patch in the series, [PATCH 07/10], specifically targets the drm/gem module and replaces __attribute__((nonnull)) with __nonnull_args(). This change is intended to keep attribute quirks in one place rather than having them scattered throughout the code.

review_comments.author: Andy Shevchenko
review_comments.summary: Initially suggested that the patch might be unnecessary, but later retracted this comment and suggested cleaning up headers that pull compiler_types/compile_attributes directly.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 02:00:28PM +0100, Miguel Ojeda wrote:
> On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 8:32\u202fAM Thomas Zimmermann <tzimmermann@suse.de> wrote:
> >
> > Should gem.h now include <linux/compiler_attributes.h> ?
> 
> No, it should be included for you (unless you are doing something
> custom with the compiler flags etc.).

Usually it comes to the mere drivers via types.h, in rare cases (usually some
more generic library headers, we do better granularity as it affects the almost
entire kernel. Just double check that types.h is explicitly included.

-- 
With Best Regards,
Andy Shevchenko

review_comments.author: Andy Shevchenko
review_comments.summary: Told the patch author to discard his previous comment, and suggested cleaning up headers that pull compiler_types/compile_attributes directly.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 01:12:06PM +0000, Dmitry Ilvokhin wrote:
> On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 02:00:28PM +0100, Miguel Ojeda wrote:
> > On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 8:32\u202fAM Thomas Zimmermann <tzimmermann@suse.de> wrote:
> > >
> > > Should gem.h now include <linux/compiler_attributes.h> ?
> > 
> > No, it should be included for you (unless you are doing something
> > custom with the compiler flags etc.).
> 
> Just to add a bit more colour to Miguel's reply.
> 
> I believe idea behind include/linux/compiler_attributes.h is to make
> attribute wrappers as simple and transparent to use as native compiler
> attributes. In particular, this means they should be available in every
> kernel compilation unit without any additional effort.
> 
> For this reason, all the nessesary plumbing is handled at the build
> machinery level (see scripts/Makefile.lib:171), where '-include'
> compiler flag is used to pull in include/linux/compiler_types.h, which
> in turn pulls include/linux/compiler_attributes.h.

Ah, TIL! Please, discard my comment then. Perhaps we need to clean up all
headers that pull compiler_types/compile_attributes directly (the same way
we do for kconfig.h).

-- 
With Best Regards,
Andy Shevchenko

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series replaces open-coded uses of the __attribute__((nonnull)) macro with the __nonnull_args() macro, which is a wrapper that keeps the quirks of the attribute in one place. The goal is to standardize nonnull attribute usage across the Linux kernel tree. The patches can be applied separately and are build-tested on various configurations. Some instances of __attribute__((nonnull)) remain in the tools subdirectory and should be updated separately after this patchset lands.

On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 02:00:28PM +0100, Miguel Ojeda wrote:
> On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 8:32\u202fAM Thomas Zimmermann <tzimmermann@suse.de> wrote:
> >
> > Should gem.h now include <linux/compiler_attributes.h> ?
> 
> No, it should be included for you (unless you are doing something
> custom with the compiler flags etc.).

Just to add a bit more colour to Miguel's reply.

I believe idea behind include/linux/compiler_attributes.h is to make
attribute wrappers as simple and transparent to use as native compiler
attributes. In particular, this means they should be available in every
kernel compilation unit without any additional effort.

For this reason, all the nessesary plumbing is handled at the build
machinery level (see scripts/Makefile.lib:171), where '-include'
compiler flag is used to pull in include/linux/compiler_types.h, which
in turn pulls include/linux/compiler_attributes.h.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 01/12] mm/page_alloc: reset can_retry_reserves when the slowpath restarts
series_items.patch_summary: The patch series aims to improve the page allocation mechanism in the Linux kernel by resetting the can_retry_reserves flag when the slowpath restarts after a cpuset update or zonelist rebuild. This ensures that an allocation attempt is made at most once per change, preventing potential issues with reclaiming memory.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch as correct, added Acked-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> Commit 2c4c3e29897d ("mm/page_alloc: simplify __alloc_pages_slowpath()
> flow") retries an allocation once with reserve_flags when the caller
> becomes eligible for reserves, guarded by can_retry_reserves.
>
> A restart after a cpuset update or a zonelist rebuild retries with
> can_retry_reserves already set to false, so a caller that cannot
> reclaim (GFP_NOWAIT | __GFP_MEMALLOC), fails without trying reserves.
>
> Reset can_retry_reserves on restart. Only a cpuset or zonelist change
> restarts the slowpath, so the retry still runs at most once per change.
>
> With a kprobe helping to make the race deterministic, an allocation
> can be made to return NULL. With this patch the allocation will succeed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 02/12] mm/page_alloc: keep the pagesets of an empty zone
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prevents the pagesets of an empty zone from being freed prematurely, which can cause corruption when a new owner takes over the per-cpu memory. series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the accuracy of oom detection tracepoints by passing the zone pointer instead of the zoneref pointer in the reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint. This change is necessary due to memory hotplug rebuilds, which can cause the zonelist entries to move and result in incorrect zone identification.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 04/12] mm/page_alloc: detect zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the Linux kernel's memory management by detecting and handling zonelist rebuilds from memory hot-add operations. The first patch in the series addresses a specific issue where concurrent allocation failures can occur due to spurious allocation failures caused by zonelist rewrites during node onlining.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch without raising any concerns or objections.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
> presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.
>
> However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
> onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
> in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
> allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.
>
> For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
> rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:
>
>   [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
>
> A concurrent GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_THISNODE allocation can observe the
> intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
> CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
> allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.
>
> Gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every
> configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.
>
> Fixes: 3d36424b3b58 ("mm/page_alloc: fix race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation")
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
> ---
>  mm/page_alloc.c | 4 ++--
>  1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)
>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 05/12] mm/mmzone: read the zoneref slot once in zonelist_zone()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory hotplug rebuilds of zonelists in place, which can lead to inconsistent zone references. The patch introduces READ_ONCE() to ensure a single load of the zoneref slot in zonelist_zone(). This change is necessary to prevent double-put bugs and maintain reference counts.

review_comments.author: Zi Yan
review_comments.summary: Identified the patch as correct and suitable for inclusion in the kernel. Acknowledged the need to ensure a single load of the zoneref slot.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat Oct 31, 2026 at 10:13 PM EDT, Gregory Price (Meta) wrote:
> Memory hotplug rebuilds zonelists in place while allocations walk them,
> so a zoneref slot can change between two loads of it.
>
> zonelist_zone() loads the slot with a plain access.  The compiler may
> load it again later instead of keeping the zone it already read, so a
> caller can check one zone and then use another, or the NULL terminator.
>
> Use READ_ONCE().  Callers that take a zone from a slot and keep using
> it, such as get_page_from_freelist() with ac->preferred_zoneref, need
> that single load.
>
> Fixes: 11cd8638c37f ("mm, page_alloc: remove stop_machine from build_all_zonelists")

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 06/12] mm/page_alloc: snapshot the preferred zone against shrink rebuilds
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a kernel NULL pointer dereference bug in the page allocator by reading the preferred zone only once, instead of re-reading it at every use. This is achieved by introducing a snapshot of the preferred zone against concurrent zonelist rebuilds. The fix involves modifying the get_page_from_freelist() function to store the preferred zone in a local variable and using this variable throughout the function.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 08/12] mm/page_alloc: retry allocations that raced with a zonelist rebuild
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where GFP_KERNEL allocations can land in the wrong zone due to concurrent zonelist rebuilds. It introduces a new function, `check_retry_zonelist`, which checks if the zonelist has changed since the allocation was made and retries the allocation if necessary. This is done by freeing the allocated page and retrying the allocation. The patch also adds a new function, `zonelist_iter_sample`, which samples the zonelist sequence number without waiting for the writer to finish. This allows for faster allocation paths to detect concurrent rebuilds and retry allocations accordingly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 09/12] mm/hugetlb: retry the pool walk when the zonelist is rebuilt
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem where a hugetlb fault bound to one node can take a pool page from another due to the way the zonelist is rebuilt during zone onlining. The patch introduces checks for zonelist updates and retries the pool walk if the zonelist has changed, ensuring that pages are taken from the correct node. This change fixes an issue where kprobes holding the walk across the online could cause a fault to take a page from the wrong node.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 10/12] mm/page_alloc: retry alloc_contig_pages() when the zonelist is rebuilt
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses issues related to the allocation of contiguous pages in the Linux kernel's memory management system. Specifically, it introduces a retry mechanism when the zonelist is rebuilt during zone online operations. This change aims to prevent gigantic hugetlb pages from being allocated in ZONE_MOVABLE and ensures that the correct zone is used for page allocation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 11/12] mm/mempolicy: read the zoneref slot once in mempolicy_slab_node()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a double-put bug in the mm/mempolicy module by reading the zoneref slot only once in mempolicy_slab_node(). This change is necessary to prevent kernel oopses when a movable block goes offline.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses memory hotplug-related races and issues in the Linux kernel's memory allocator. The patches fix problems such as zone list rebuilds, page set freeing, and allocation failures that can occur when memory is added or removed from a system while allocations are happening. The approach taken involves fixing specific walkers and functions to ensure correct behavior during these operations, including removing a helper function that invites the same bug. The patches were tested on a QEMU guest with three NUMA nodes and showed improved results compared to an unmodified kernel.

review_comments.author: Gregory (Meta) (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern that the zonelist_update_seq retry should not be limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE, as this can cause spurious allocation failures for __GFP_THISNODE callers when onlining zones. The author agrees and explains that build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, shifting entries in every zonelist containing a zone being onlined.
review_comments.raw_body:
Commit 2c4c3e29897d ("mm/page_alloc: simplify __alloc_pages_slowpath()
flow") retries an allocation once with reserve_flags when the caller
becomes eligible for reserves, guarded by can_retry_reserves.

A restart after a cpuset update or a zonelist rebuild retries with
can_retry_reserves already set to false, so a caller that cannot
reclaim (GFP_NOWAIT | __GFP_MEMALLOC), fails without trying reserves.

Reset can_retry_reserves on restart. Only a cpuset or zonelist change
restarts the slowpath, so the retry still runs at most once per change.

With a kprobe helping to make the race deterministic, an allocation
can be made to return NULL. With this patch the allocation will succeed.

Fixes: 2c4c3e29897d ("mm/page_alloc: simplify __alloc_pages_slowpath() flow")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>

 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

index a8cac5e01066..f1048168c90c 100644
--- a/mm/page_alloc.c
+++ b/mm/page_alloc.c
@@ -4783,7 +4783,7 @@ __alloc_pages_slowpath(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order,
 	unsigned int zonelist_iter_cookie;
 	int reserve_flags;
 	bool compact_first = false;
-	bool can_retry_reserves = true;
+	bool can_retry_reserves;
 	unsigned long alloc_start_time = jiffies;
 
 	if (unlikely(nofail)) {
@@ -4805,6 +4805,7 @@ __alloc_pages_slowpath(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order,
 	no_progress_loops = 0;
 	compact_result = COMPACT_SKIPPED;
 	compact_priority = DEF_COMPACT_PRIORITY;
+	can_retry_reserves = true;
 	cpuset_mems_cookie = read_mems_allowed_begin();
 	zonelist_iter_cookie = zonelist_iter_begin();

From: Josef Bacik <josef@toxicpanda.com>

should_reclaim_retry() walks a zonelist and passes the zoneref pointer
to the reclaim_retry_zone tracepoint, which loads the zone from the
entry again to find the node.

Memory hotplug rebuilds the zonelists in place while allocations are
under way. When a zone in front of the zoneref entry has become empty,
the entries move up, and this one can be the end marker by the time the
tracepoint looks at it. zonelist_node_idx() then dereferences a NULL
zone. Short of that, the event can name another zone than the one its
numbers belong to.

Pass the zone pointer instead of the zoneref pointer.

Fixes: d379f01de095 ("oom, trace: add oom detection tracepoints")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Assisted-by: LLM

-	TP_PROTO(struct zoneref *zoneref,

 		int order,

@@ -41,7 +41,7 @@ TRACE_EVENT(reclaim_retry_zone,
 		int no_progress_loops,

-	TP_ARGS(zoneref, order, reclaimable, available, min_wmark, no_progress_loops, wmark_check),
+	TP_ARGS(zone, order, reclaimable, available, min_wmark, no_progress_loops, wmark_check),

@@ -55,8 +55,8 @@ TRACE_EVENT(reclaim_retry_zone,

+		trace_reclaim_retry_zone(zone, order, reclaimable,

2.56.0

---

The zonelist_update_seq retry was limited to CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE,
presumably because only hot-remove takes zones out of a zonelist.

However, build_zonerefs_node() rewrites the zonelists in place, so
onlining the first block of a zone shifts the entries that follow it
in every zonelist containing that zone.  This can cause a spurious
allocation failure for a __GFP_THISNODE caller.

For a node with only ZONE_NORMAL, onlining its first ZONE_MOVABLE block
rewrites the node's ZONELIST_NOFALLBACK list as:

  [NORMAL, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NULL] -> [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]

A concurrent GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_THISNODE allocation can observe the
intermediate list, skip ZONE_MOVABLE, and find no eligible zone. With
CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE=n, check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 and the
allocation fails even though the node has free ZONE_NORMAL memory.

Gate the sequence checks on CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG, which covers every
configuration that rebuilds zonelists after boot.

Fixes: 3d36424b3b58 ("mm/page_alloc: fix race condition between build_all_zonelists and page allocation")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
---
 mm/page_alloc.c | 4 ++--
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

diff --git a/mm/page_alloc.c b/mm/page_alloc.c
index e14d550d4128..11be12b443ad 100644
--- a/mm/page_alloc.c
+++ b/mm/page_alloc.c
@@ -4404,7 +4404,7 @@ static DEFINE_SEQLOCK(zonelist_update_seq);
 
 static unsigned int zonelist_iter_begin(void)
 {
-	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE))
+	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG))
 		return read_seqbegin(&zonelist_update_seq);
 
 	return 0;
@@ -4412,7 +4412,7 @@ static unsigned int zonelist_iter_begin(void)
 
 static unsigned int check_retry_zonelist(unsigned int seq)
 {
-	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTREMOVE))
+	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG))
 		return read_seqretry(&zonelist_update_seq, seq);
 
 	return seq;
-- 
2.56.0

From: Josef Bacik <josef@toxicpanda.com>

When the last memory of a zone goes offline, zone_pcp_reset() frees
zone->per_cpu_pageset and zone->per_cpu_zonestats. Nothing waits for those
who found the zone populated and still use the two pointers. They take
neither the memory hotplug lock nor any other lock which offline_pages()
holds, and some of them can sleep:

  CPU0 vmstat_update()                CPU1 offline_pages()
  refresh_cpu_vm_stats()
    for_each_populated_zone(zone)
      pcp = zone->per_cpu_pageset
      cond_resched()
                                      adjust_present_page_count()
                                      zone_pcp_reset(zone)
                                        free_percpu(zone->per_cpu_pageset)
      decay_pcp_high(zone, pcp)
      __this_cpu_write(pcp->expire, 0)

The same goes for drain_all_pages(NULL), which takes pcp->lock, for
zone_pcp_update(), show_free_areas() and the readers and writers of the
zonestats. If the per-cpu memory has got a new owner in the meantime, it
is corrupted.

The pagesets are only freed because setup_zone_pageset() would otherwise
leak them when the zone gets memory again. Keep them instead and let
setup_zone_pageset() and zone_pcp_init() use them again, like it is done
with pgdat->per_cpu_nodestats. Their lists are empty, and their limits
have been calculated for a zone without memory by the
init_per_zone_wmark_min() of offline_pages(), which is what
setup_zone_pageset() would come up with as well.

Fixes: 340175b7d14d ("mm/hotplug: free zone->pageset when a zone becomes empty")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Assisted-by: LLM
Signed-off-by: Josef Bacik <josef@toxicpanda.com>
Signed-off-by: David Hildenbrand (Arm) <david@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>
Signed-off-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
---
 mm/page_alloc.c | 20 ++++++++++++++------
 1 file changed, 14 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)

diff --git a/mm/page_alloc.c b/mm/page_alloc.c
index f1048168c90c..1850a41f24f7 100644
--- a/mm/page_alloc.c
+++ b/mm/page_alloc.c
@@ -6308,6 +6308,10 @@ void __meminit setup_zone_pageset(struct zone *zone)
 {
 	int cpu;
 
+	/* The zone has been populated before, see zone_pcp_reset(). */
+	if (zone->per_cpu_pageset != &boot_pageset)
+		return;
+
 	/* Size may be 0 on !SMP && !NUMA */
 	if (sizeof(struct per_cpu_zonestat) > 0)
 		zone->per_cpu_zonestats = alloc_percpu(struct per_cpu_zonestat);
@@ -6400,6 +6404,10 @@ void __init setup_per_cpu_pageset(void)
 
 __meminit void zone_pcp_init(struct zone *zone)
 {
+	/* A node which is added again, see zone_pcp_reset(). */
+	if (zone->per_cpu_pageset && zone->per_cpu_pageset != &boot_pageset)
+		return;
+
 	/*
 	 * per cpu subsystem is not up at this point. The following code
 	 * relies on the ability of the linker to provide the
@@ -7680,6 +7688,12 @@ void zone_pcp_enable(struct zone *zone)
 	mutex_unlock(&pcp_batch_high_lock);
 }
 
+/*
+ * The zone has become empty. Its pagesets and zonestats are not freed: nothing
+ * keeps somebody who found the zone populated, such as refresh_cpu_vm_stats()
+ * or drain_all_pages(), from still using them. They are used again when the
+ * zone gets memory again.
+ */
 void zone_pcp_reset(struct zone *zone)
 {
 	int cpu;
@@ -7690,12 +7704,6 @@ void zone_pcp_reset(struct zone *zone)
 			pzstats = per_cpu_ptr(zone->per_cpu_zonestats, cpu);
 			drain_zonestat(zone, pzstats);
 		}
-		free_percpu(zone->per_cpu_pageset);
-		zone->per_cpu_pageset = &boot_pageset;
-		if (zone->per_cpu_zonestats != &boot_zonestats) {
-			free_percpu(zone->per_cpu_zonestats);
-			zone->per_cpu_zonestats = &boot_zonestats;
-		}
 	}
 }
 
-- 
2.56.0

---

Memory hotplug rebuilds zonelists in place while allocations walk them,
so a zoneref slot can change between two loads of it.

zonelist_zone() loads the slot with a plain access.  The compiler may
load it again later instead of keeping the zone it already read, so a
caller can check one zone and then use another, or the NULL terminator.

Use READ_ONCE().  Callers that take a zone from a slot and keep using
it, such as get_page_from_freelist() with ac->preferred_zoneref, need
that single load.

Fixes: 11cd8638c37f ("mm, page_alloc: remove stop_machine from build_all_zonelists")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
---
 include/linux/mmzone.h | 3 ++-
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/include/linux/mmzone.h b/include/linux/mmzone.h
index ecd1ebd49756..4bc2318ac37f 100644
--- a/include/linux/mmzone.h
+++ b/include/linux/mmzone.h
@@ -1855,7 +1855,8 @@ extern struct zone *next_zone(struct zone *zone);
 
 static inline struct zone *zonelist_zone(struct zoneref *zoneref)
 {
-	return zoneref->zone;
+	/* Memory hotplug rewrites zonelists in place. */
+	return READ_ONCE(zoneref->zone);
 }
 
 static inline int zonelist_zone_idx(const struct zoneref *zoneref)
-- 
2.56.0

---

__next_zones_zonelist() tests a slot's zone for NULL, then reads the
slot again to look up the zone's node. Offlining a zone's last block
rebuilds the zonelists in place, so the second read can return the
terminator:

  CPU 0                             CPU 1
  __next_zones_zonelist(nodemask)
    zonelist_zone(slot 1) = NORMAL
                                    offline_pages()
                                      build_all_zonelists()
                                        [MOVABLE, NORMAL, NULL]
                                        -> [NORMAL, NULL]
    zref_in_nodemask(slot 1)
      zone_to_nid(NULL)

Current GCC and clang merge the two reads, but nothing requires it.
With mm/mmzone.o built with -fno-inline -fno-ipa-sra, holding a
nodemask allocation between the reads while the node's last movable
block goes offline oopses every time:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000060
  RIP: 0010:zone_to_nid+0x0/0x10
  Call Trace:
   zref_in_nodemask+0x9/0x20
   __next_zones_zonelist+0x23/0x70
   prepare_alloc_pages.constprop.0+0x16c/0x190
   __alloc_frozen_pages_noprof+0xaf/0x330

Read the slot once and test that zone. A NULL zone still ends the walk.

Fixes: 11cd8638c37f ("mm, page_alloc: remove stop_machine from build_all_zonelists")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>
---
 mm/mmzone.c | 11 ++++++-----
 1 file changed, 6 insertions(+), 5 deletions(-)

diff --git a/mm/mmzone.c b/mm/mmzone.c
index 9cc9ef588580..65880396f104 100644
--- a/mm/mmzone.c
+++ b/mm/mmzone.c
@@ -43,13 +43,14 @@ struct zone *next_zone(struct zone *zone)
 	return zone;
 }
 
-static inline int zref_in_nodemask(struct zoneref *zref,
-				   const nodemask_t *nodes)
+/* A NULL zone terminates the zonelist, so it ends the search. */
+static inline bool zone_in_nodemask(const struct zone *zone,
+				    const nodemask_t *nodes)
 {
 #ifdef CONFIG_NUMA
-	return node_isset(zonelist_node_idx(zref), *nodes);
+	return !zone || node_isset(zone_to_nid(zone), *nodes);
 #else
-	return 1;
+	return true;
 #endif /* CONFIG_NUMA */
 }
 
@@ -67,7 +68,7 @@ struct zoneref *__next_zones_zonelist(struct zoneref *z,
 			z++;
 	else
 		while (zonelist_zone_idx(z) > highest_zoneidx ||
-				(zonelist_zone(z) && !zref_in_nodemask(z, nodes)))
+		       !zone_in_nodemask(zonelist_zone(z), nodes))
 			z++;

---

Onlining the first block of a zone rebuilds every zonelist in place,
shifting the slots after the new zone.  The iterator approves a slot,
then the allocator loads the zone from it, so a GFP_KERNEL request can
land in ZONE_MOVABLE and a nodemask request on a node outside its mask:

  CPU 0                             CPU 1
  prepare_alloc_pages()
    first_zones_zonelist(nodemask {1})
      slot 0 (NORMAL1) approved
                                    online_pages()
                                      build_all_zonelists()
                                        [NORMAL1, NORMAL2, ...]
                                        -> [MOVABLE1, NORMAL1, ...]
  get_page_from_freelist()
    zone = zonelist_zone(slot 0)    /* MOVABLE1 */
    allocates from MOVABLE1

zonelist_update_seq detects the rebuild, but only the slowpath's failure
exits check it.

Check it whenever an allocation succeeds too, and if it changed, free
the page and retry, as the memcg charge failure path does.  Eligible
pages are dropped as well: zonelists only change when memory comes or
goes, and a retry is simpler than rechecking the page.

Freeing the page does not undo a block the allocation claimed.  A
GFP_KERNEL request that lands in a fresh ZONE_MOVABLE converts a free
block to MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE, which stays until the zone's movable free
list runs out and a movable allocation takes it back.

The fast and bulk paths read the seqlock's raw seqcount without waiting:
an ALLOC_NOLOCK caller can be an NMI that interrupted the writer, and on
PREEMPT_RT the seqlock accessor takes the spinlock.  A sample taken
mid-write costs a retry, or NULL under ALLOC_NOLOCK.
check_retry_zonelist() returns 0 when compiled out, so a backport
without the hot-add change stays harmless.

Fixes: 11cd8638c37f ("mm, page_alloc: remove stop_machine from build_all_zonelists")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>
---
 mm/page_alloc.c | 34 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++-
 1 file changed, 33 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)

diff --git a/mm/page_alloc.c b/mm/page_alloc.c
index 28d46f987685..f2f7e96bdef2 100644
--- a/mm/page_alloc.c
+++ b/mm/page_alloc.c
@@ -4419,12 +4419,25 @@ static unsigned int zonelist_iter_begin(void)
 	return 0;
 }
 
+/*
+ * Never wait for the writer, which an ALLOC_NOLOCK caller in NMI may have
+ * interrupted. Read the raw seqcount: on PREEMPT_RT the seqlock accessor takes
+ * the spinlock while a write is in progress.
+ */
+static unsigned int zonelist_iter_sample(void)
+{
+	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG))
+		return raw_seqcount_begin(&zonelist_update_seq.seqcount.seqcount);
+
+	return 0;
+}
+
 static unsigned int check_retry_zonelist(unsigned int seq)
 {
 	if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG))
 		return read_seqretry(&zonelist_update_seq, seq);
 
-	return seq;
+	return 0;
 }
 
 /* Perform direct synchronous page reclaim */
@@ -5100,6 +5113,12 @@ __alloc_pages_slowpath(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order,
 	warn_alloc(gfp_mask, ac->nodemask,
 			"page allocation failure: order:%u", order);
 got_pg:
+	/* A rebuild during the walk may have handed out an ineligible zone. */
+	if (page && check_retry_zonelist(zonelist_iter_cookie)) {
+		__free_frozen_pages(page, order, FPI_NONE);
+		page = NULL;
+		goto restart;
+	}
 	return page;
 }
 
@@ -5184,6 +5203,7 @@ unsigned long alloc_pages_bulk_noprof(gfp_t gfp, int preferred_nid,
 	struct list_head *pcp_list;
 	struct alloc_context ac;
 	unsigned int alloc_flags = ALLOC_WMARK_LOW;
+	unsigned int zonelist_iter_cookie;
 	int nr_populated = 0, nr_account = 0;
 
 	/*
@@ -5224,6 +5244,7 @@ unsigned long alloc_pages_bulk_noprof(gfp_t gfp, int preferred_nid,
 	/* May set ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT, fragmentation will return 1 page. */
 	gfp &= gfp_allowed_mask;
 	gfp = current_gfp_context(gfp);
+	zonelist_iter_cookie = zonelist_iter_sample();
 	if (!prepare_alloc_pages(gfp, 0, preferred_nid, nodemask, &ac, &gfp, &alloc_flags))
 		goto out;
 
@@ -5273,6 +5294,10 @@ unsigned long alloc_pages_bulk_noprof(gfp_t gfp, int preferred_nid,
 	if (unlikely(!zone))
 		goto failed;
 
+	/* The zone was chosen from a zonelist that a rebuild may have changed. */
+	if (unlikely(check_retry_zonelist(zonelist_iter_cookie)))
+		goto failed;
+
 	/* spin_trylock may fail due to a parallel drain or IRQ reentrancy. */
 	pcp = pcp_spin_trylock(zone->per_cpu_pageset);
 	if (!pcp)
@@ -5413,6 +5438,7 @@ struct page *__alloc_frozen_pages_noprof(gfp_t gfp, unsigned int order,
 		.alloc_flags = alloc_flags,
 	};
 	unsigned int fastpath_alloc_flags = alloc_flags;
+	unsigned int zonelist_iter_cookie;
 
 	/* Other flags could be supported later if needed. */
 	if (WARN_ON(alloc_flags & ~(ALLOC_NOLOCK | ALLOC_NO_CODETAG)))
@@ -5442,6 +5468,7 @@ struct page *__alloc_frozen_pages_noprof(gfp_t gfp, unsigned int order,
 	 */
 	gfp = current_gfp_context(gfp);
 	alloc_gfp = gfp;
+	zonelist_iter_cookie = zonelist_iter_sample();
 	if (!prepare_alloc_pages(gfp, order, preferred_nid, nodemask, &ac,
 			&alloc_gfp, &fastpath_alloc_flags))
 		return NULL;
@@ -5458,6 +5485,11 @@ struct page *__alloc_frozen_pages_noprof(gfp_t gfp, unsigned int order,
 
 	/* First allocation attempt (or, for nolock, only attempt) */
 	page = get_page_from_freelist(alloc_gfp, order, fastpath_alloc_flags, &ac);
+	if (likely(page) && unlikely(check_retry_zonelist(zonelist_iter_cookie))) {
+		__free_frozen_pages(page, order,
+				    alloc_flags & ALLOC_NOLOCK ? FPI_NOLOCK : 0);
+		page = NULL;
+	}
 	if (likely(page) || (alloc_flags & ALLOC_NOLOCK))
 		goto out;

The author added checks for zonelist updates and restarts the walk if it changed. This change fixes a fault bound to one node taking a page from another in 3 out of 3 runs with kprobes holding the walk across the online.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a performance regression caused by outdated automatic interleave weights in the Linux kernel's memory policy module (mm/mempolicy). When nodes gain or lose memory, their weights are not recalculated from their reported bandwidths, leading to an uneven distribution of data and potential overload. The patch introduces a new function, wi_state_refresh(), which recomputes the weights based on the recorded bandwidth whenever a node gains or loses its first/last memory. If allocating new weights fails, it warns once and continues with the next recompute starting from the full bandwidth table.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a divide error and panic issue in the weighted interleave auto-tuning mechanism by recording nodes visited while summing bandwidth and using that same set when scaling and reducing weights, ensuring consistent state even if N_MEMORY changes.

>
> From: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
>
> Switching weighted interleave back to automatic mode while memory is
> being onlined can cause a kernel divide error on x86, and a panic if
> panic_on_oops is set.

> reduce_interleave_weights() scans N_MEMORY three times, but hotplug
> can cause N_MEMORY to change at runtime - and torn reads on that
> nodemask can cause a total sum of zero bandwidth.  A node that

> loop to generate a div/0.
>
> Record the nodes visited while summing their bandwidth, then use
> that same set when scaling and reducing the weights.  This gives
> us a consistent state even if N_MEMORY changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/4] btrfs: honor FMODE_NOCMTIME in btrfs_write_check()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the btrfs_write_check function to honor the FMODE_NOCMTIME flag, which prevents updating the inode's c/mtime when writing files over NFSv4.2. This is necessary because nfsd sets this flag on files with delegated timestamps, and skipping the update ensures that the server's c/mtime does not become newer than the time reported by the delegation holder. The patch fixes a stat-dirty file issue found in git test t1092.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/4] btrfs: honor FMODE_NOCMTIME when punching holes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where Btrfs was updating the c/mtime of files even when FMODE_NOCMTIME was set, which can cause problems for NFS clients holding delegated timestamps. The patch introduces a new function btrfs_should_update_cmtime() to determine whether c/mtime should be updated based on file mode and flags. It then uses this function in btrfs_write_check() and replaces the update_times flag with an argument in btrfs_replace_file_extents(). Finally, it updates btrfs_punch_hole() to skip c/mtime updates for FMODE_NOCMTIME files. This patch fixes a regression introduced by a previous commit that froze c/mtime updates during WRITE_ATTRS delegation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/4] btrfs: honor FMODE_NOCMTIME in fallocate
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Btrfs file system where fallocate operations would update the inode's ctime and mtime even when FMODE_NOCMTIME is set, which prevents such updates. The patch introduces an 'update_times' flag that is passed from btrfs_fallocate() to its helpers, ensuring that these times are only updated when necessary. Additionally, it increments the inode's i_version unconditionally in btrfs_fallocate_update_isize(), as this operation can change the NFS change attribute even if the size extension stays within existing preallocation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/4] btrfs: honor FMODE_NOCMTIME when cloning
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Btrfs file system where cloned files would always update their creation and modification times, even when FMODE_NOCMTIME was set. This is problematic because it allows a client to advance the server's ctime during a CLONE operation, which can cause issues with delegated timestamps. The patch makes btrfs_clone_files() respect FMODE_NOCMTIME by passing no_time_update for destinations that have this flag set. Additionally, it exposes the btrfs_should_update_cmtime() function to reflink.c so that it can be used in other contexts.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes issues in the Btrfs file system where it did not properly handle the FMODE_NOCMTIME flag, which is used to prevent modification of timestamps. The patches correct this behavior in several places, including btrfs_write_check(), punching holes, fallocate, and cloning operations. This fix was tested with the git regression testsuite and is intended for inclusion in Linux kernel version 7.5.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to ensure that multigrain timestamps are working correctly in Linux kernels. The test, called 'mgtime', checks that the mtime and ctime of a file appear to change even when there are multiple writes in quick succession. This is particularly important for filesystems like ext4, f2fs, btrfs, tmpfs, and xfs, which support multigrain timestamps but may not be universally supported on all filesystems. The test uses a loop to write to a file 1000 times and then checks that the mtime and ctime are different from the previous value each time. If the values do not change, the test fails.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 4/4] mm: add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list, addressing a memory regression issue on systems under pressure. The change mirrors existing behavior for PMD-sized folios and ensures that zero-filled mTHPs can be split and reclaimed. A minimum size threshold of 2M is set to balance overhead and effectiveness.

review_comments.author: Barry Song
review_comments.summary: Reiterated a previously agreed-upon decision to use a hardcoded 2MB size threshold for underused splitting. Provided a Reviewed-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Nov 4, 2026 at 5:20 AM Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Unlike for PMD-sized folios, an anonymous mTHP folio doesn't get added
> to the deferred split list at fault or collapse time. As a result, a
> fully mapped mTHP folio that is mostly zero-filled doesn't get split by
> the deferred split shrinker when the system is under memory pressure.
>
> At Meta we would like to deploy 2M THP=always on arm64 with 64k base
> pages, as 2M gives the contpte benefits while the PMD size (512M) is too
> big to use. Without underused splitting this causes memory regressions,
> as the unused parts of those folios can never be broken down and
> reclaimed.
>
> Add anonymous mTHP folios to the deferred split list from
> map_anon_folio_pte_nopf(), mirroring what map_anon_folio_pmd_nopf()
> already does for PMD-sized folios. This covers both the fault path and
> the khugepaged mTHP collapse path. If there is memory pressure, a
> zero-filled mTHP can then be split with its zero pages remapped to the
> shared zero page and reclaimed.
>
> Only queue mTHP folios of at least 2M for underused splitting. With
> thp_underused() scaling khugepaged/max_ptes_none to the folio size, any
> folio of order 2 or above could in principle be underused, but for small
> folios it is unlikely to be worth it. An order-2 folio on 4k base pages
> can free at most four pages and on systems that only enable small mTHP
> sizes (eg Android's order-2-only configuration) zero-filled subpages
> tend to be few and short-lived.
>
> The minimum is hard-coded rather than a knob, since admins have no good
> way of choosing it, and is a size rather than an order since what a
> split recovers depends on the folio's size in bytes, and the same order
> means very different sizes across different base page sizes. It can be
> lowered later if data shows smaller sizes are worth it. PMD-sized folios
> are exempt from the minimum in order to maintain backwards compatibility
> since on some architectures (s390, with a 1M PMD) the PMD size can be
> below 2M.
>
> To minimize overhead on the common order-0 fault path, the
> deferred_split_folio() call is guarded by an inline folio_test_large()
> check.
>
> Suggested-by: Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev>
> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
> ---

I believe we discussed this before and agreed that a
hardcoded 2MB would be a better starting point.

Reviewed-by: Barry Song <baohua@kernel.org>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 1/3] mm: zswap: fix shrinker count for the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the zswap shrinker, which incorrectly scales the number of freeable entries on the root memcg's LRU by its compression ratio. The issue arises because the root memcg's stats don't account for its own entries, leading to incorrect scaling and potential data loss. To fix this, the patch uses the zswap pool-wide counters for the root memcg instead, ensuring that all entries are properly accounted for.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: Acknowledged the patch for dropping the unnecessary flush operation and applied it with an Acked-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Mon, Nov 2, 2026 at 2:51 PM Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> zswap_shrinker_count() scales the number of freeable entries on a
> memcg's zswap LRU by the memcg's compression ratio. That compression
> ratio is computed from the memcg's MEMCG_ZSWAP_B and MEMCG_ZSWAPPED
> stats.
>
> However, for the root memcg, the zswap entries owned by the root memcg
> itself are never accounted for in the stats (obj_cgroup_charge_zswap()
> skips the root objcg, and before the root memcg had an objcg, its
> entries weren't charged at all). The stats only reflect the entries
> owned by the root memcg's descendants. When the root memcg's descendants
> have no zswap entries (eg when the whole workload runs in the root
> cgroup), the shrinker reports nothing to reclaim for the root memcg, and
> its zswap entries are never written back by the shrinker. When its
> descendants do have entries, the root memcg's entries are scaled by the
> descendants' compression ratio instead of a ratio that includes them.
>
> Fix this by using the zswap pool-wide counters for the root memcg
> instead. The zswap pool-wide counters cover every zswap entry, including
> those owned by the root memcg.
>
> This also gets rid of having to flush the root memcg's stats, which
> flushes every cgroup in the system.

I would have taken the patch just for the dropped flush ;)

>
> In a VM running a reclaim-heavy workload in the root cgroup with the
> zswap shrinker enabled, the shrinker wrote back no pages before this
> change (zswpwb stayed at 0) and 1016 pages with it.
>
> Fixes: b5ba474f3f51 ("zswap: shrink zswap pool based on memory pressure")
> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>

Acked-by: Yosry Ahmed <yosry@kernel.org>

Thanks!

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 2/3] mm: memcg: read root lruvec LRU stats from the node counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the accuracy of LRU (Least Recently Used) statistics in the Linux kernel's memory cgroup (memcg) subsystem by reading the root lruvec LRU stats from the node counters instead of relying on potentially stale rstat flushes. This change is particularly important for global reclaim and refault detection, where accurate statistics are crucial. The patch introduces two new functions, `lruvec_lru_page_state` and its monotonic variant, which read the node counters for the root memcg. This approach eliminates the latency introduced by rstat flushes, reducing the time taken to perform root reclaim from approximately 0.9ms to near-zero. The change also improves the accuracy of LRU statistics, ensuring that they reflect the current state of memory allocation and deallocation in the system.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Yosry Ahmed suggested that the patch could be simplified by directly using the node counters in lruvec_page_state() and lruvec_page_state_monotonic(), as these functions already fallback to node stats when memcg is disabled. They asked if there are cases where the node stats would not be suitable.
review_comments.raw_body:
Why not do this directly in lruvec_page_state() and
lruvec_page_state_monotonic()? They already fallback to node stats if
memcg is disabled, why not do the same for the root? Are there cases
where the node stats are not the right thing to do?

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that there are cases where node counters and root memcg stats may not be equal, specifically citing slab's NR_SLAB_RECLAIMABLE_B and NR_SLAB_UNRECLAIMABLE_B statistics, and explained that this is due to the way slab pages are accounted for in the node counter but only updated in the memcg stats under certain conditions.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Yosry,

Thanks for taking a look at this series! I don't think we're able to
do this directly in lruvec_page_state()/lruvec_page_state_monotonic()
because I think there's still some places where the node stat and the
root memcg stat are not guaranteed to be equal.

The stat I was looking at last week was slab's NR_SLAB_RECLAIMABLE_B
and NR_SLAB_UNRECLAIMABLE_B where for those, the node counter value
can contain memory/stats that wasn't actually charged to any memcg,
which I think means for these cases, the node counter values can be
larger than what reading the root memcg rstat value would give. The
functions I was looking at were account_slab() and
memcg_slab_post_alloc_hook() where the logic adds every new slab page
to the node counter but the memcg stats only get updated if specific
criteria are met (eg the cache had SLAB_ACCOUNT set or the allocation
had the __GFP_ACCOUNT gfp flag set and the allocation was not from a
root memcg).

Thanks,
Joanne

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary: Reviewer suggested special casing slab stats to read from node counters by default, eliminating the need for a flush.
review_comments.raw_body:
If it's only the slab stats, it probably makes sense to special case
those instead of the rest of the readers, right? It would be nice if
the default behavior is reading the node stats that doesn't require a
flush.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledges that additional statistics would need to be excluded from the special casing, and is open to either approach (special casing or using a separate helper) for v2.
review_comments.raw_body:
If we were to special case it, it would need to exclude more than a
couple, I think. I asked a LLM and it says NR_KERNEL_STACK_KB,
NR_PAGETABLE, NR_SECONDARY_PAGETABLE, NR_VMALLOC, NR_HUGETLB,
WORKINGSET_NODERECLAIM would also need to be excluded. We could add
this special casing in, but we would need to make sure any new stat
that gets added in the future that belongs on the exclusion list gets
put on it. If it's missed, the failure would be silent whereas with a
separate helper, callers have to explicitly opt in. I'm happy to go
either way though, so if there's one way you prefer, I'm happy to do
that for v2.

Thanks,
Joanne

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed questioned the distinction made in the patch between 'root memcg stats' and 'node stat', wondering if it's intentional for all statistics, specifically pointing out that memory.stat draws a similar distinction.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed questioned whether the distinction between root memcg stats and node stats is intentional, suggesting that the default behavior should be to have them as the same, and proposed an explicit opt-out approach.
review_comments.raw_body:
Interesting. So for all these stats, root memcg stats (from
memory.stat) is not the same as the node stat? They all draw a
distinction between "accounted to root" vs "not accounted"? I wonder
if this is intentional for all of them.

---

I think we probably want to first understand if these stats are
supposed to be different between the root memcg stats and the node
stats first. Personally, I think the default should be the majority
behavior, which I think is that node stats and root memcg stats are
the same, so I am leaning toward explicit opt-out. Let's also see what
memcg folks think.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author Joanne Koong addressed a concern about how kernel memory allocations are accounted for in the root cgroup, explaining that some allocations (category b) should be linked to the root memcg and others (category a) shouldn't be. She wondered if the original commit's decision to not track kernel memory pages to a given memcg was due to avoiding extra overhead costs.

Author agrees that the suggestion is reasonable and asks for input from other memcg developers.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think there's 2 categories:
a) the allocation isn't acccounted to any memcg (eg kernel page
tables, hugetlb when hugetlb accounting is off, unaccounted slab
caches and kmallocs w/out __GFP_ACCOUNT, and most vmalloc). These
values only get added to the node counter

b) the allocation is accounted, but it comes from a task running in
the root cgroup (eg kernel stacks, user + secondary page tables,
accounted slab, etc)

I think a) has to stay as is since it's not linked to any memcg. For
b), it seems intentional from the original commit that added kernel
memory accounting logic (commit 7ae1e1d0f8ac ("memcg: kmem controller
infrastructure")). The commit message for that explicitly says
tracking kernel memory pages to a given memcg "will happen whenever
the caller includes the flag __GFP_KMEMCG flag and the task belongs to
a memcg other than the root". (__GFP_KMEMCG later became
__GFP_ACCOUNT). I wonder though if this was to avoid extra overhead
costs (eg for systems that don't use cgroups) on the hot paths, since
it would need to do non-trivial per-object work. If root read the node
counters for the stats that are in category b (excluding the stats
that are in both category a and b) instead of going through rstat
(which is what this series does for the LRU stats), there wouldn't
need to be any extra overhead at allocation time, since nothing would
need to be tracked.

---

That seems reasonable to me. memcg folks, do you have any thoughts on this?

Thanks,
Joanne

series_items.subject: [PATCH v1 3/3] mm/damon/core: use node counters instead of flushing the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series modifies the DAMOS core to use node counters instead of flushing the root memcg for LRU size calculations. The change is made to improve performance by reducing unnecessary flushes, which can occur frequently in common use cases.

review_comments.author: SJ Park
review_comments.summary: The reviewer approved the patch with minor reservations, noting that it looks good but there may be edge cases where users use different quota settings for the root memcg. They suggested that some users might use DAMOS_QUOTA_NODE_MEM_{USED,FREE}_BP instead of flushing the root memcg.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Joanne,


On Mon,  2 Nov 2026 14:50:30 -0800 Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:

> damos_get_node_memcg_used_bp() flushes the memcg stats before reading
> the LRU sizes of the goal's memcg on the goal's node. For the root
> memcg, that flushes every cgroup in the system. The flush is not
> ratelimited, which means it happens every time the goal is evaluated.

Just thinking loudly.  damos_get_node_memcg_used_bp() is called only once per
DAMOS quota reset interval.  It is usually recommended to set the interval to 1
second.  So a sort of rate limiting is applied in common use cases.  That said,
some users might using quite short interval.  And it is obviously better to
avoid unnecessary flushes.

> 
> For the root memcg, the node counters hold the same LRU sizes as the
> memcg rstat stats, and they are always up to date. Use
> lruvec_lru_page_state(), which reads the node counters for the root
> memcg, and skip the flush for the root memcg.

Again, loud thought.  For root memcg, users might use
DAMOS_QUOTA_NODE_MEM_{USED,FREE}_BP instead, which calls
damos_get_node_mem_bp().  That said, some users might use
DAMOS_QUOTA_NODE_MEMCG_{USED,FREE}_BP for root memcg (maybe it makes user space
tool writing easier?).

So, looks all good to me, thank you for this patch.

> 
> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>

Assuming the discussion on patch 2 concludes to have lruvec_lru_page_state(),

Reviewed-by: SJ Park <sj@kernel.org>


Thanks,
SJ

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses the issue of memcg stats flushing, which can be costly and introduce staleness in statistics. For the root memcg, it's possible to directly read global counters instead of going through rstat, as they are always up-to-date. patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch moves the updates of LRU size statistics out of the lru_lock critical section in folio batches, which reduces contention and improves throughput. The stats are accumulated while holding the lock and applied after dropping it, reducing the overhead of cache misses and improving performance. This change is particularly beneficial for workloads with many threads faulting and freeing memory in a single memcg, where the hold time of lru_lock directly limits throughput. The patch also moves cost_lock into the hole after lru_lock to make room for the batch pointer, keeping struct lruvec from growing. The stats may lag behind the LRU lists by one batch, but this is within the per-cpu batching already present.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/5] fuse: convert ext_map iomap ops to ->iomap_next()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series converts the fuse ext_map iomap operations to use the new ->iomap_next() callback, which is generated using the DEFINE_IOMAP_ITER_NEXT() macro. This change does not introduce any functional changes and only updates the iomap operation callbacks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/5] iomap: remove ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end() legacy path
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the legacy ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end() path in the iomap code, as all in-tree filesystems have implemented the ->iomap_next() method. The changes involve updating the iomap_iter function to use the ->iomap_next() method instead of the legacy path and removing the corresponding flags and functions from the iomap_ops structure. This change simplifies the iomap code and reduces its complexity.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/5] iomap: pass iomap_iter_next_fn directly instead of struct iomap_ops
series_items.patch_summary: This patch simplifies the iomap code by removing the struct iomap_ops, which only contained a single function pointer. Instead, the iomap_iter_next_fn is passed directly to the iomap_iter and other entry points. This change is possible because all filesystems now implement ->iomap_next() and have removed the legacy fallback. The patch also renames the ops field in the iomap_iter tracepoint to next for consistency.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/5] Documentation: iomap: update docs to reflect iomap_iter_next model
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the iomap documentation to reflect a change in how filesystems interact with the iomap API. Specifically, it removes support for separate ->iomap_begin() and ->iomap_end() callbacks, replacing them with a single iomap_iter_next() callback that finishes the previous mapping (if any) and produces the next one. The patch updates documentation across three files to reflect this change.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series converts various filesystems to use the new iomap_iter_next model, which replaces the legacy ->iomap_begin() and ->iomap_end() functions. The patches are rebased on current mainline and include preparatory patches for nilfs2 and fuse iomap code. The changes also update documentation to reflect the new model. The series applies cleanly to both current mainline and next-20261027, but conflicts may arise by the time it is picked up at the end of the merge window.

Re: [PATCH v2] mm: move LRU size stat updates out of lru_lock in folio batches
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: Joanne Koong posted a v3 of the patch addressing David Hildenbrand's suggestion to add documentation about a potential race condition between reparenting and stats updates.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong
review_comments.summary: Posted a v3 addressing David Hildenbrand's suggestion to add documentation about a potential race condition between reparenting and stats updates.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, Nov 5, 2026 at 11:53 AM Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Thu, Nov 5, 2026 at 11:37 AM David Hildenbrand (Arm)
> <david@kernel.org> wrote:
> >
> > On 10/30/26 01:19, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> > > On Thu, Oct 29, 2026 at 01:41:57PM -0700, Joanne Koong wrote:
> > >> folio_batch_move_lru() and folios_put_refs() take the lruvec's lru_lock
> > >> once per batch, but they update the node and memcg lruvec stats for
> > >> every folio in the batch while holding the lock. Only the LRU lists and
> > >> the memcg lru_zone_size need lru_lock. Updating the stats while holding
> > >> the lru_lock is unnecessary, and they make up a large part of the
> > >> critical section, as seen in [1] where a change that added just a few
> > >> instructions to the memcg stat update path cost about 2% throughput
> > >> because the LRU stat updates run under lru_lock, and the overhead went
> > >> away once they were moved outside of the lock.
> > >>
> > >> With many threads faulting and freeing memory in a single memcg, about
> > >> half of all cycles are spent waiting for lru_lock, and the hold time of
> > >> the lru_lock directly limits throughput. A perf profile with 80 threads
> > >> faulting in and freeing shmem in a single memcg shows 52.8% of all
> > >> cycles spent spinning on lru_lock, split evenly between
> > >> folio_batch_move_lru() and folios_put_refs(). About 25% of the time
> > >> spent holding lru_lock in those two paths goes to the LRU stat updates,
> > >> mostly cache misses loading pn->memcg, pn->lruvec_stats_percpu and the
> > >> per-cpu counters. The stat updates are only 0.7% of all cycles, but they
> > >> lengthen the critical section that the other threads are waiting on.
> > >>
> > >> Accumulate the stat changes per LRU list while holding the lock instead,
> > >> and only apply them after dropping the lock (while still inside
> > >> the RCU read section that keeps the lruvec's memcg alive). This moves
> > >> the stat updates out of the lru_lock critical section and turns the
> > >> per-folio updates into at most one update per LRU list per batch.
> > >
> > > This updating of stats after dropping the lru lock does introduce one behavior
> > > change i.e. race between reparenting on offlining and stats update. I think it
> > > is safe and correct though. Better to document it.
> > >
> > >>
> > >> The batch is attached to the lruvec while lru_lock is held so that the
> > >> LRU add/del helpers don't need to pass it down. To keep struct lruvec
> > >> from growing, cost_lock is moved into the hole after lru_lock, which
> > >> leaves room for the batch pointer in the same cacheline as lru_lock.
> > >>
> > >> The stats can now lag behind the LRU lists by one batch, which is well
> > >> within the per-cpu batching they already have.
> > >>
> > >> On a 2-socket Skylake (80 CPUs, 2 NUMA nodes), with threads pinned to
> > >> CPUs repeatedly faulting in and freeing memory in a single memcg,
> > >> average pages per second over 7 freshly created memcgs per run, 2 boots
> > >> each:
> > >>
> > >>                      before    after
> > >>   shmem, 20 threads  4.74M     5.47M   (+15%)
> > >>   shmem, 80 threads  7.94M    10.33M   (+30%)
> > >>   anon,  20 threads  3.04M     3.35M   (+10%)
> > >>   anon,  80 threads  3.23M     3.41M   (+5%)
> > >>
> > >> Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-fsdevel/CAJnrk1ZezmmzrYdf8KP6re_a76izMS=qGPeC8ZZXiteHyZZC-Q@mail.gmail.com/ [1]
> > >> Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
> > >
> > > Acked-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>
> > >
> >
> > Thanks, I'm planning on queue this.
> >
>
> I'll send out a v3 today that adds the documentation Shakeel suggested
> about the race between reparenting on offlining and stats update.
>

I'm seeing that the patch was picked up yesterday into mm-new. Could
you or Andrew add this paragraph to the commit message after the
"Accumulate the stats changes..." paragraph?:

"Applying the stats after dropping lru_lock means a batched update can
race with reparenting when the memcg is being offlined. This is ok
because updates to a dying memcg are redirected to its nearest
non-dying ancestor, which is where its folios end up after
reparenting."

Apologies for any inconveniences.

Thanks,
Joanne

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 1/7] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: The patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in mm/memcontrol.c by flattening nested page_counter operations, making the control flow easier to follow and reducing complexity.

review_comments.author: Balbir Singh
review_comments.summary: Acked the patch without raising any concerns or suggestions.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 2/7] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, similar to memcg's seven-slot per-CPU stock. It adds a new struct page_counter_stock_pcp that preserves the existing behavior from memcg and includes a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and its owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this patch, which is part of a larger series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 3/7] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior in !allow_spinning scenarios, where charges are made as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots. The second parameter reflects the size of a successful hierarchy charge, used for memory.high accounting heuristics.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 4/7] mm/memcontrol: check PF_MEMALLOC after trying the limits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of memory charging in Linux to check for PF_MEMALLOC after trying limits, rather than before. This change is necessary because a later patch moves the memory stock into the page counter, leaving no room between consuming the stock and trying limits for the PF_MEMALLOC check. The patch checks for PF_MEMALLOC on both outcomes of the page counter charge, skipping memory.high on success and forcing the charge on failure.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 5/7] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more efficient and accurate memory management. The change preserves the legacy user-visible relationship between memory and swap usage, even when their raw values temporarily diverge. It also introduces a new logic to prevent reclaiming swap space when both memory and swap have equal limits. The patch removes unused code from memcg and prepares it for future work on introducing additional page counters without breaking the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 6/7] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), which handles both stocks uniformly. If memory charge fails, only the nr_pages from memsw are rolled back. This change enables the raw counters for memory and memsw to temporarily drift due to cached amounts, while preserving the user-visible cgroup-v1 invariant.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v8 7/7] mm/memcontrol: restrict memory stock to leaf cgroups on v2
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts memory stock to leaf cgroups in the new page_counter_stock world, ensuring that stock does not get stranded in the hierarchy and cannot be used by processes that actually charge. It achieves this by preventing stock from accumulating in non-leaf page_counters through three methods: clearing the parent's memory stock pointer, scheduling drains for non-isolated CPUs, and lazily cleaning up CPUs that are not drained due to isolation or racing with a refill. The patch also re-enables stock when a parent becomes a leaf again.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the stock implementation from memcontrol to page_counter, allowing for better separation of charge caching and policy management. The stock is a per-CPU cache of precharged pages that speeds up small allocations by avoiding frequent walks of the page_counter hierarchy. By moving it to page_counter, the patch simplifies the handling of stock in non-leaf cgroups and prepares for future improvements. It also ensures that locking behavior remains unchanged and that exact charging is preserved for non-spinning callers.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/2] arm64: sdei: Run the event handler on the kernel vectors
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes an issue where SDEI events dispatched to the kernel vectors in user space cause a CPU hang due to undefined instruction exceptions. The patch installs the kernel vectors in the __sdei_handler function when VBAR_EL1 holds trampoline vectors, and restores it before returning to firmware. This ensures that exceptions taken by the handler execute correctly and do not loop forever. Additionally, this change covers irqentry_nmi_enter() and irqentry_nmi_exit(), which can also take an exception. The patch addresses a problem where SDEI events dispatched in user space cause CPU hangs due to undefined instruction exceptions.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author acknowledged that the current implementation of __sdei_handler() does not handle the case where VBAR_EL1 holds the trampoline vectors, and explained how they plan to fix this by switching to the kernel vectors when necessary.

review_comments.author: Catalin Marinas
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that irqs_disabled() may be false due to preempt debugging and pseudo-NMIs, which would cause a warning in __this_cpu_read(), and suggested using raw_cpu_read() or saving/restoring PMR and priorities similar to kernel_entry code.
review_comments.raw_body:
Sashiko had a comment that the above should be raw_cpu_read() since with
preempt debugging and pseudo-NMIs, irqs_disabled() is false here and the
check in __this_cpu_read() will warn.

Thinking about it, further down on the irqentry_nmi_enter() ->
lockdep_hardirqs_off() we'll hit the irqs_disabled() issue again. We
could just do a raw_local_irq_save/restore() around this function.
Unnecessary for DAIF but useful with pseudo-NMIs.

Alternatively, __sdei_asm_handler() could save/restore PMR and change
the priorities similar to the kernel_entry code. Actually, this may be
better since do_sdei_event() also checks regs_irqs_disabled() and we
don't have any regs->pmr populated.

Worth a separate patch to fix SDEI handling with pseudo-NMI on and no
changes to __this_cpu_read() above needed. So, for this patch:

Reviewed-by: Catalin Marinas <catalin.marinas@arm.com>

(I'll probably queue it for -rc but waiting to see if there are more
comments)

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/2] arm64: sdei: Preserve the interrupted context's exception registers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where SDEI events can interrupt the kernel, causing exception registers to be overwritten and leading to incorrect behavior. The patch saves the interrupted context's exception registers (ELR, SPSR, ESR, and FAR) in the __sdei_handler function before entering NMI context and restores them after exiting NMI context. This prevents nested exceptions from being harmful if their handlers are safe in NMI context, and warns about any other exception class.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author acknowledged a concern that the interrupted context's exception registers were not being saved and restored correctly in __sdei_handler(). They explained that this was necessary to prevent overwriting of the ELR, SPSR, ESR, and FAR registers. The author confirmed that they had added code to save these registers before irqentry_nmi_enter() and restore them after irqentry_nmi_exit(), making it safe for nested exceptions in NMI context.

review_comments.author: Breno Leitao
review_comments.summary: The reviewer tested the patch on NVIDIA Grace with SDEI firmware, KASAN + lockdep, and reported that it fixed a crash caused by a task interrupted in el0t_64_sync getting the handler's BRK, followed by lockdep/KASAN fallout and a hard lockup. They confirmed that the patch produced no warnings or stalls under stress testing.
review_comments.raw_body:
Tested-by: Breno Leitao <leitao@debian.org>

Tested on NVIDIA Grace (firmware SDEI) with next-20261104, KASAN + lockdep,
ARM_SDEI_NMI=y: sysrq-l under stress-ng, with a kprobe on show_regs() and
eprobes on irq_disable/irq_enable that fault on purpose.

Without the series the box crashed (a task interrupted in el0t_64_sync
got the handler's BRK, then lockdep/KASAN fallout and a hard lockup)

With it, KPTI off and kpti=1, ~4000 kprobe hits and ~5500 faults in
irqentry_nmi_enter()/exit() produced no warnings or stalls.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses an issue where SDEI events can cause exceptions in the event handler, leading to unexpected behavior and crashes. The patches modify the SDEI event handling code to run the handler on kernel vectors instead of trampoline vectors, which are not suitable for synchronous exceptions. Additionally, the patches save and restore exception registers around the event handler to prevent overwriting of interrupted context's registers. This change improves the robustness of SDEI event handling and prevents issues such as CPU stalls, SIGILL, and SIGSEGV in user tasks.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author acknowledged that the IRQ-like resume into user space must still go through the trampoline to map the kernel, and confirmed that the patch series addresses the issue of exceptions taken by the handler breaking the interrupted context.
review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

An SDEI event can land anywhere, and a synchronous exception taken by its
handler breaks the context it interrupted:

 - With KPTI, an event that lands in user space runs the handler on the
   trampoline vectors, whose current-EL half is empty. The exception
   loops there and the CPU is lost.

 - The exception overwrites ELR, SPSR, ESR and FAR. If the event landed
   in exception entry or return, the interrupted context runs on the
   handler's values: a task gets SIGILL, or the kernel oopses on a fault
   it never took.

Patch 1 runs the handler on the kernel vectors. Patch 2 saves and
restores the exception registers around it.

Handlers take such exceptions in normal operation now that SDEI delivers
NMI backtraces: show_regs() reads through _nofault() accessors that
fault, and a kprobe or WARN anywhere in the path takes a BRK.

Tested under QEMU TCG with TF-A, 4 CPUs, 20 x sysrq-l under load, with a
test-only copy_from_kernel_nofault() of address 0x10 in
sdei_nmi_handler():

 - v7.4-rc1, KPTI on: CPUs stuck in the trampoline vectors, RCU stalls.
 - v7.4-rc1, KPTI off: 60 "unsafe: exception during handler" warnings,
   SIGILL and SIGSEGV in user tasks, and an oops in execve().
 - With the series, KPTI on and off: no warnings, no stalls. The same
   with an eprobe on irq_disable that reads address 0x10, which faults
   inside irqentry_nmi_enter() when the event lands in user space.

An earlier revision of patch 2 was also run on arm64 hardware with
firmware SDEI, where a plain sysrq-l was enough to trigger the warning
without it.

  https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261104180936.2981070-1-kas@kernel.org/

   before irqentry_nmi_enter(), and restore them after
   irqentry_nmi_exit(). Both can take an exception too: the eprobe above
   wedged v1 with KPTI on (Usama). do_sdei_event() takes the interrupted
   VBAR for the IRQ-like resume.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v2 01/18] mm: free PG_rcu_free folios only after an RCU grace period
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new page flag, PG_rcu_free, which allows folios to be freed only after an RCU (Read-Copy Update) grace period. This is done to prevent CPUs from bouncing the reference count of a page cache folio while it's being read by multiple processes. The flag is 64-bit only and is disabled on PREEMPT_RT kernels where expedited grace periods are normal. A new workqueue, WQ_MEM_RECLAIM, is used to free batches of pages after an RCU grace period has passed. This patch also introduces a new counter in /proc/vmstat to track the number of deferred pages.

review_comments.author: David (Arm)
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer David suggested renaming PG_rcu_free to FOLIO_RCU_FREE, aligning it with the existing naming convention for folio-specific flags.

Reviewer David (Arm) noted that the patch description does not accurately describe what the basic infrastructure in page_alloc does, and suggested adding a dedicated FOLIO_RCU_FREE config to enable pagecache use.

Reviewer David suggested replacing the PG_rcu_free flag definition with a const mask constructed using BIT() and __PG_RCU_FREE to avoid a growing list of flags, which would be more consistent with other page flags.

Reviewer David suggested moving the handling of PG_rcu_free to mm/folio.c, specifically intercepting on the folio freeing path in __folio_put() before free_frozen_pages(), which is used by other machinery such as slab.
review_comments.raw_body:
I think we really want to focus this only on folios (like the current code does).

FOLIO_RCU_FREE ?

---

While that description is helpful, that's not really what this patch, or rather
the basic infrastructure in page_alloc, does.

I'd suggest to have a dedicated FOLIO_RCU_FREE config and maybe another one
(that selects/depends on) FOLIO_RCU_FREE that actually enables the pagecache use
and documents the details.

---

That looks a bit odd at first, as it's very different to the other once. But no
easy way around assuming that the flag is not always around.

Maybe we should just have this be a const mask constructed somewhere using BIT()
and __PG_RCU_FREE etc, instead of having this growing list in this user here.

---

I'm wondering whether we want to intercept on the folio freeing path instead?
That would be __folio_put(), before we go into free_frozen_pages() used by other
machinery that does not apply (slab etc).

So maybe this handling could be placed into mm/folio.c instead, just a quick
thought ... reading about folio batches above I think that might be the right
direction, we are mixing too much page vs. folio things here.
